tier_reason: Every number in claimed_speedup appears in the libriscv/kvmserver README (Rust 13 vs 28 us, Deno hello 17 vs 50 us, React 646 vs 695 us, 55 us reset and 80 us of 690 us overhead) with the CPU model (Ryzen 9 7950X) and Deno 2.3.6 stated. The harness (examples/bench.ts) is public, but the published tables compare only against native. The win over fork, V8 isolates and WebAssembly is a prose claim from 'previous experiments' with no table, and compiler flags are not stated, so the tier is C.

corrections.baseline: per-request sandboxing by process fork, a new V8 isolate or WebAssembly (Wasmtime serve); native Linux process as the speed reference. kvmserver's examples/bench.ts has benchmark groups for Wasmtime serve (instance reuse on/off and release), Bun process forking and Node isolated-vm isolate-per-request, but the README publishes no results for them
corrections.caveats: The varnish/tinykvm README and docs (docs/ holds only arm64-feature-matrix.md and seccomp.md) have no benchmark, only the qualitative claim that programs run 'at the same speed' in TinyKVM. The numbers come from libriscv/kvmserver, a separate project in the libriscv organization whose recent commits are by lrowe. They measure kvmserver plus TinyKVM, not TinyKVM alone. kvmserver's examples/bench.ts defines Wasmtime serve, Bun process-forking and Node isolated-vm per-request groups, but the README publishes only native and kvmserver tables. The 1.5-2 orders of magnitude claim over fork, V8 isolates and WebAssembly therefore rests on 'previous experiments' with no published table. Per request it is slower than native (Rust 13 vs 28 us, Deno hello world 17 vs 50 us, React 646 vs 695 us). Compiler flags are not stated. Snippets from search results (HN, Medium; snippet only) mention about 2.5 us snapshot restore and roughly 0.4 ms extra latency for React rendering in an earlier proof of concept; neither was used as evidence. The license is GPL-3.0 only, with a commercial dual licence from Varnish Software, and contributors must sign a CLA.

notes: Record is accurate. Kept at C: the measured baseline is native (and slower), and the claimed win over fork, V8 isolates and Wasm has no published numbers even though kvmserver's bench.ts can run those baselines. A rerun of that harness's Wasmtime, Bun fork and isolated-vm groups would be what could lift it. License GPL-3.0 confirmed from the LICENSE text, 823 stars, last commit 2026-08-21 (fwsGonzo).

tier_reason: docs/BENCHMARKS.md has first-party CI and local tables, but they only compare the repo's own JIT build with its own interpreter build and packaging variants. That is stock OTP BeamAsm against the stock emu flavor, not BEAM.com against stock Erlang/OTP. There are no numbers against a recognizable incumbent, so the tier stays D.

corrections.caveats: Nothing in the repo shows BEAM.com beating stock Erlang/OTP. The BeamAsm JIT it ships is the one stock OTP already has on x86_64 and aarch64, so the fib gains (2.3x on Linux x86_64, about 11.6x on Linux aarch64) are JIT against interpreter, not against the incumbent BEAM. The measurements are first-party, from shared CI machines with noise it puts at about 10%, with no CPU model or compiler flags. The gate tables carry only relative limits. The JIT build starts 40 to 90 ms slower than the interpreter build. The only part faster by design is the packaging: one portable file, and storing kernel and stdlib uncompressed starts about 27% faster than its own all-compressed variant (193-202 ms to 143-146 ms). Its WebAssembly build (docs/WORKERS.md) runs Erlang code at 1.2 to 1.4 times the time of the native interpreter in Node.js, so it is slower there. The repo bundles Erlang/OTP, Elixir, Cosmopolitan Libc, OpenSSL, SQLite and WAMR under their own licenses (NOTICE, licenses/). It is not a C++ library. Kept as tier D because no recognizable baseline is beaten.

notes: The numbers in claimed_speedup match BENCHMARKS.md (Linux x86_64 fib 70 to 30, lists 249 to 116, binary 249 to 133, maps 83 to 68, ets 70 to 64, messages 111 to 117; aarch64 fib 139 to 12, lists 411 to 104, binary 290 to 91). They are an internal JIT-vs-emu comparison, not a win over stock OTP. Shortcomings: no comparison against stock Erlang/OTP, 0 stars, Erlang packaging project rather than C++, and the Wasm build is slower than native. Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-10-06, active.

The chain_plugin docs list the --eos-vm-oc-enable (default auto), --eos-vm-oc-whitelist (default xsat,vaulta), cache-size and compile-threads options without performance numbers. The EOSIO v2.0.0 release notes call OC a 'high performance WASM tier-up runtime' and say the background compile takes 'a handful of seconds', with no numbers. The 'often an order of magnitude faster' than WABT, Binaryen, EOS VM interpreter and EOS VM JIT claim comes from search-result snippets of the EOS VM documentation (snippet only), with no workload, hardware or compiler. An everstake.one blog on CPU execution time could not be opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED). OC is embedded in the node and is not a standalone library. Tier D by the assignment rule; the eos-vm repo is catalogued separately. The last commit on main is 2025-11-12 (a LICENSE update); release dates on the releases page could not be pinned to a year with certainty.

notes: Record is accurate; the only change is fuller caveats (WAVM BSD-3 notice in the OC directory, OC enabled by default only for whitelisted accounts, no numbers in the release notes or docs). Shortcomings: no benchmark or numbers anywhere reachable, claim known only from doc snippets, and it is embedded in a blockchain node rather than a standalone library.
